content:
ON THE HUNT—Veteran ghost hunter Richard Senate speaks Aug. 27 to members of the Avenue Library Ghosthunters Club in Ventura. Senate, who has spent decades investigating reports of paranormal activity, said his experiences have made him more—not less—open to the unexplained. SCOTT STEEPLETON/Acorn Newspapers

Richard Senate started looking for ghosts expecting eventually to explain them away.

Decades later, the longtime pursuer of the paranormal says the opposite happened.

“When I first got into this, I thought there had to be a scientific reason behind it all—something to explain it away,” Senate said. “The more and more I got into it, the more spiritual I became.”

Senate shared stories and lessons from a lifetime investigating the paranormal Aug. 27 with a couple dozen people gathered for a meeting of the Avenue Library Ghosthunters Club in Ventura. Some in the room had years of unexplained experiences behind them. Others were newcomers, curious about the paranormal and how people go about investigating it.

A smattering of guests represented another generation entirely: They had grown up hearing about Senate and his ghostly exploits from their parents and came simply for the chance to meet the man behind the stories.

Senate, who has written about ghosts and other unexplained phenomena up and down the state, had something for everyone. He shared tales of local sightings, recalled firsthand experiences from fabled sites like the Whaley House in San Diego and Queen Mary in Long Beach and even recounted the investigation that would have sent a lesser hunter to the hospital.

His first piece of advice for aspiring ghost hunters was decidedly practical: Take pictures. Lots of them.

“Take 40 or 50,” Senate said.

Digital photography has made that easier, he said. Unlike the days of film, investigators can take dozens of photographs without worrying about developing them and simply erase those that show nothing unusual.

Senate recalled one photograph taken in the children’s room of a building said to be haunted by a little girl. The image appeared to show a smiling girl reflected in the mirror of a cabinet.

More intriguing to Senate was what she appeared to be holding.

At first he thought the object looked like a violin or small guitar. He enlarged the photograph and showed it to musicians, who told him it resembled a small guitar-like instrument used in some musical groups, including mariachi ensembles.

The position of the girl’s hand appeared to Senate to correspond with how the instrument would actually be played. “Evidently, this is a memory or something,” he said, “but it’s the most weird picture I’ve ever seen.”

Senate’s fascination with the paranormal has taken him from Civil War battlefields to California missions and historic sites across Ventura County.

Battlefields such as Gettysburg, Antietam and Shiloh have long histories of reported paranormal activity, he said. California escaped much of that kind of bloodshed, although Senate has investigated the site of the Battle of San Pasqual near San Diego.

Closer to home, Senate pointed to two destinations with reputations for paranormal activity: the Glen Tavern Inn in Santa Paula and Nordhoff Cemetery in Ojai.

The Glen Tavern dates to Santa Paula’s days as an oil boomtown. Senate recounted stories of its third floor being used for illicit drinking, gambling and prostitution during an era when local authorities attempted to rein in the rowdy behavior accompanying the influx of oil workers.

Senate said visitors have reported seeing the figure of a woman looking from a third-floor window. According to the story, the woman once served as a lookout, watching for police so those inside could hide the alcohol and otherwise make themselves presentable before officers arrived.

“That was her station,” Senate said, adding that reports of her apparition continue.

Senate said he has spent considerable time investigating the Glen Tavern, including Room 308, sometimes referred to as the Houdini Room. Other unusual activity has been reported on the third floor.

Nordhoff Cemetery offers another place for people interested in local ghost lore.

Senate has conducted nighttime tours of the Ojai cemetery, where visitors have reported unusual experiences. With its standing monuments rather than the predominantly flat markers of many modern cemeteries, he said, Nordhoff can resemble an old Western “Boot Hill.”

Senate has chronicled many such places in books including “The Haunted Southland,” an older, now out-of-print volume covering paranormal stories and locations around Southern California.

The crowd let out a collective gasp when Senate shared the time he fell through a trap door while investigating ghost stories at one home, a mishap that sent him home with a huge bruise and scrapes and cuts.

But after decades of collecting stories, conducting tours and investigating purported hauntings, Senate said the fundamental question has changed.

When he began, belief in ghosts was more likely to draw a joke than serious consideration.

“Most people didn’t believe in ghosts,” he said. People would tease him about studying “goats” instead.

Today, he believes the subject is more accepted.

“Now, more people believe that there’s a phenomenon,” Senate said. “The big question is, what is it, not if it exists, because too many people, over too many centuries, have seen too many things.” Senate pointed to reports from people he considers credible, including doctors and philosophers, as evidence that accounts of strange encounters cannot all be dismissed as intoxication or imagination.

But what those people actually experienced remains an open question.

“What are they seeing? Ah, that’s the rub,” Senate said.

He rattled off possibilities: time warps, imagination, projection, even interdimensional travel or something resembling the multiverse theory.

“We don’t know,” Senate said. “But it’s a mystery I hope to solve someday. Or at least try.”

The search has changed Senate’s own thinking about life and death.

He now leans toward a spiritualist philosophy in which physical death is not necessarily the end. He likened life to “a big giant school,” where people learn lessons and improve themselves before moving to another level.

His thinking incorporates elements of reincarnation—returning to learn lessons again when necessary—and a series of levels of spiritual advancement.

Senate readily acknowledged it as a theory rather than an answer.

“I don’t know,” he said. “That’s kind of where I’m at at this point in my life.”

And there is still humor in his version of the afterlife.

In Senate’s evolving theory, reaching the next level does not mean spending eternity sitting on a cloud playing a harp. There is more living, learning and apparently even employment.

“Guess what?” Senate said. “You have to get a job.”

An eternity on a cloud, he said, sounds as though “it’d be boring after a while.”

Senate has been telling ghost stories, leading tours and investigating purported hauntings around Ventura County for decades. When he retired from the City of Ventura, he noted, a building was named for him—an honor he recognizes as unusual.

But recognition is not what has kept him searching.

“I like to have fun doing the stuff,” Senate said. “I’m still very passionate about it. I haven’t sort of lost the zeal.”
